articleTitle: IEE Colloquium on 'Recent Advances in Broadcast TV Cameras - Optics, Sensors and Processing' (Digest No.040)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Recent Advances in Broadcast TV Cameras - Optics, Sensors and Processing
IEE Colloquium on Recent Advances in Broadcast TV Cameras - Optics, Sensors and Processing
abstract: The lens on the front of a television camera is the first in a long line of subsystems which together make up a TV broadcast system. Its performance, together with that of the camera, will have a very significant bearing on the final image which the observer sees. This paper reviews briefly the main optical parameters to be assessed, and discusses some of the current and imminent challenges with which one is faced when measuring these parameters.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: From 525/625 TV lines to HDTV, the evolution of optical requirements for TV cameras
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Recent Advances in Broadcast TV Cameras - Optics, Sensors and Processing
abstract: Two important requirements make HDTV lenses different from present television lenses. First the picture is wider, and although the image may be scanned over the same sensor diagonal, the 16:9 aspect ratio necessitates better correction of distortion. Secondly the quality of HDTV has to be twice as good; the same MTF must be maintained, although the spatial frequency is doubled. While this level of performance is not new to the optical designer who has already been involved with photography or motion pictures, the task is considerably more difficult because of the following constraints: (1) good camera sensitivity requires high aperture optics; (2) operational requirements dictate long zoom ranges; and (3) a beam-splitting prism is located between the lens and the sensors. This paper explores in some detail what is needed and what can be done in order that the lens does not limit the HDTV system's performance.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Specifications for film and television camera lenses
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Recent Advances in Broadcast TV Cameras - Optics, Sensors and Processing
abstract: The first part of this paper deals with definitions, measuring conditions, presentation of results, and equipment for carrying out measurements. The second part relates typical test results that can be obtained when the performance of lenses is measured in accordance with the procedures described. Some guidance is given on the effect of the various lens errors in the picture, and advice is offered concerning the specific requirements on camera lenses according to their application.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A user's view: technical and ergonomic limitations of current systems. (broadcast TV cameras)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Recent Advances in Broadcast TV Cameras - Optics, Sensors and Processing
abstract: The last twelve months have seen the introduction of CCDs into the full facility studio or outside broadcast camera. The BBC decided that only the frame interline or frame transfer CCD would offer high enough overall quality. The author discusses limitations still present on these camera systems, dealing first with the technical and then with the ergonomic aspects.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Aspects of digital signal processing in broadcast cameras
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Recent Advances in Broadcast TV Cameras - Optics, Sensors and Processing
abstract: Broadcast cameras remain the final area in the production chain to incorporate digital signal processing. Digital effects, mixers, VTRs and lately even digital routeing are all accepted in the broadcast environment. This paper examines the background to the success of digital processing, the difficulties of applying such technology to cameras, and the benefits which such a digital camera would bring to users.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
